newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean troops kill suspected N.Korean commandos.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean troops kill suspected N.Korean commandos.

text.p: Two suspected North Korean infiltrators as well as South Korean soldiers were killed on Tuesday in fierce exchanges of gunfire in the country's rugged east coast mountains, Seoul officials said.

The suspected infiltrators were shot dead after they opened fire with M-16 automatic rifles and hurled grenades at pursuing South Korean soldiers near the border with the communist North, a Defence Ministry spokesman said.
"We think the two killed today came from the submarine," he said, referring to a North Korean submarine which landed 26 agents on the South's east coast in September.

Twenty-two of the 26 North Koreans had been killed before Tuesday in a manhunt launched after the sub landing on September 17. Another, Lee Kwang-soo was captured alive. and three were still being sought.
"We have yet to confirm the two (killed on Tuesday) are from the submarine. We are sending Lee Kwang-soo to the scene to identify them," he said.
The Shark-class submarine ran aground off the eastern city of Kangnung as it tried to pick up three spies it offloaded two days earlier, according to Lee.
A senior military officer said about 10 South Korean soldiers were killed or wounded by hand grendades thrown by the suspected agents.
"There were deaths and injuries on our side," he said, without giving details, and added that an announcement would be made later in the day.
State radio said three South Koreans -- a colonel, a captain and a corporal -- were killed and nine wounded.
The Defence Ministry spokesman said the suspected infiltrators were wearing South Korean military uniforms and carried the kind of rifles used in the South.
"But they used bullets which did not carry serial numbers. All ammunition used by our side bear serial numbers," he said.

The spokesman said South Korean special forces had been combing the rugged east coast mountains just south of the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) since Monday when the two suspected infiltrators fled after being stopped by southern soldiers.
The DMZ was set up between the two Koreas under the 1953 armistice agreement that ended the three-year Korean War. The two Koreas are still technically at war.
Tension has remained high on the peninsula, the world's last cold war frontier, since the North Korean submarine intruded into South Korea.
Tuesday's exchange of fire occurred as the United States and South Korea continued a two-week military training exercise in and around Korea against any attack from the communist North.

Rear Admiral Chales Moore, commander of the U.S. aircraft carrier Independence battle group taking part in the exercise, said last week that South Korea faced the threat of seaborne saboteurs but the United States would send aircraft to defend it if war broke out on the Korean peninsula.
The exercise, called Foal Eagle '96, involves about 34,000 U.S. troops including 10,000 seamen from the U.S. Seventh Fleet, and most of South Korea's 655,000 military personnel.

Seoul has demanded a "clear apology" from Pyongyang over the submarine incursion. North Korea has threatened to retaliate "a hundredfold or a thousandfold" over the killings and demanded the return of the bodies, the survivors and the submarine.
